  • Build performance
content_text: According to Stack Overflow, cargo is the most desired development tool. Many people attribute their choice of Rust to Cargo. I've heard from many people that Cargo is already great and that they can't think of any way it could be improved. I want to set our sights higher. And I want to hear your thoughts on what an ideal workflow would look like and how we might get there. This is just some things I've been thinking about. I know I don't know or can't easily speak to all of the workflows and others might have even better ideas on how to solve them. We can also use your help in getting there. These workflows are not isolated to just Cargo but also touch on Rust, crates.io, and more. There are plenty of opprtunities to dig in and help. Some workflows to improve I want to frame this discussion around a high level view of workflows. I'll cover specific problem areas (e.g. build scripts) as part of the ideas on how to improve them. #[non_exhaustive] Dependency management Build performance Adaptability Cargo maintenance Also, a word on agentic development Dependency management “Always bet on the ecosystem” - Battery packs: Let's talk about crates, baby I feel strongly that the crates.io ecosystem has been one of Rust's superpowers, enabling applications to be rapidly created with more capabilities and polish than would be practical without this ecosystem. Applications can leverage not just the existing functionality but any future functionality and fixes. For example, ripgrep is being optimized for large monorepos and typos automatically benefits due to reusing ignore. A fresh implementation or a fork would not see benefits like this. This also enables shared auditing. In your application, you can have one or two serialization frameworks also in use by others or you can audit ten bespoke ones spread across config systems, network communication, etc. Dependencies are not without their costs and risks which we should work to drive down. How do you discover a quality dependency? There are "known" dependencies to use, assuming you are in the know. Being productive shouldn't be gated on insider knowledge. When there isn't a "known" dependency, you are then left to find candidates which isn't always easy. To compare them, you then look for a smattering of signals to see if it is safe, fit for your purposes, and can be depended on for the long term. These may include download count, who depends on it, reviews performed, etc as well as trust carried over from other packages from the author. Knowing and aggregating these can take a lot of work. In the ideal world, all dependencies would be reviewed. We aren't in an ideal world but how do we get closer? In Rust, we have unsafe as a way to isolate code that needs further inspection. We need more types of audit points and to scale up their discoverability. Even better if you didn't need to review these audit points because they were opt-in where possible, with a fallback that didn't need audits at the cost of performance or features. Sometimes though, we will still want to take shortcuts and trust in others for reviews and tracking of our own or others' reviews should be integrated with using dependencies. How do we minimize upgrade overhead? First, we need to improve the state of linting and testing for maintainers so there are fewer bugs and unintended changes. Assuming we are now talking about intended changes, the easy answer would be to discourage breaking changes but that comes at a cost to the maintainer in not being able to clear out some types of technical debt and to users in the limits this places on features, fixes, and build performance. We should encourage documenting changes and better surface that. However, that is a stopgap that patches over the problem. How can we make this better? One source of inspiration is the Rust Language which also has a form of opt-in breaking changes through Editions. The Rust Project prepares for an edition with unstable features and by providing migrations for users. That should be viewed as the minimum experience we offer maintainers and users for packages. Going beyond that, we could better surface these changes to users, inline to their workflows and directed to their specific circumstances. This would especially be important for when migrations aren't possible. As an experiment in what can be done today, with clap I have adopted the practice of breaking changes being introduced as parallel features, deprecating the old behavior with a note in how to migrate, where possible. The deprecations have been put behind a deprecated feature flag because many people turn warnings into errors, including deprecations, and having them on by default coupled upgrading with resolving deprecations increasing costs and risks. This dramatically simplifies migration guides to "enable a feature and do what it says". Where a parallel feature isn't possible, we use an unstable-vX feature to not block development on an eventual breaking change and to make it easier to get feedback. Problems I see with this: Awareness of the deprecated feature Discovering of the migration guide The migrations are still manual unstable-vX features can have surprising effects and need more guard rails to scale up their use These are just conventions I made up; sustaining a culture around these ideas needs a paved path to raise awareness and encourage their use Build performance Improving build performance isn't about making things 2% faster but about changing how users work and making Rust attractive for more users. Users' points of comparison will range from C++, which is more similar until you account for pre-built frameworks, to scripting languages, where there are no builds. We also need to look beyond the performance of rustc to the user's workflow. Users are looking for instant feedback as they make small changes at the bottom of their stack but that unfortunately causes the entire stack to rebuild, taking some time even for cargo check. They are iterating on test failures until they get the behavior just right, either running all of cargo test --workspace in a loop ("because it's easy") or hand constructing a command like cargo test -p application-library --test area -- some::test::name for each failure to give faster iteration time at the cost of a disruption. Maybe while working through either of the above, they rebase against main and now their whole stack is rebuilding because of a dependency update. Or maybe they ran out of disk space and had to run rm -rf target. Or maybe it rebuilt for no discernible reason. Or maybe while working through either of the above, Cargo blocks on a parallel invocation, whether from rust-analyzer, another worktree they want to share the cache with, or from another project on their system that they are sharing the cache with. Some users will task switch while they wait for CI to complete so they don't stack too many changes on top of unmerged code, increasing the risk of costly merge conflicts. CI systems have caches but caching too much can negate any of the benefits due to network transit and decompression times. Defaults that work well for local debugging will increase cache sizes and slow down builds. While build results get cached, test results do not and the entire test suite re-runs. See also my RustNL 2025 presentation: video / slides Adaptability Cargo is intended to be opinionated but between that and backwards compatibility, it can be hard to be adaptable to different needs, whether that is improved docker caching, complex application needs, or integrating into a larger corporate environment. In git, they divide operations into plumbing and porcelain. Cargo is almost all porcelain commands with very limited programmatic use. Adding plumbing commands and extending the programmatic output of the porcelain commands would go a long way to enabling people to adapt Cargo to meet their needs. Cargo maintenance Underlying any talk of improving Cargo is that the Cargo team needs enough capacity to support these efforts on top of keeping the lights on. Previously, Cargo went through a several year feature freeze due to a lack of capacity from the team. I worry about how close we are to repeating that. During that feature freeze and for a while after, we had a focus on improving our processes and tooling to make us more effective in maintaining Cargo. For example, we made it easier to make sweeping UX changes by developing and migrating to a snapshot testing library that met our needs (snapbox, see #14039). Now, the thing I see slowing us down the most and limiting what we change is Cargo's architecture. Cargo is old and has bespoke frameworks, constraints on concurrent operations, uses C libraries when Rust ones can replace them, and no clear boundaries that require global knowledge when making or reviewing a change. Not everyone can fund work like that and we can only build up new design and code reviewers so quickly. Where outside contributors can most help the Cargo team is not with code but with thinking. A major enabler for thinking is to have all the context in one place by gathering all of the relevant information from the thread and summarizing it for easy consumption. For example, I have a PR on another project that slowly makes progress and when I go back to look at it, I have to refresh myself on the behavior the PR is intended to implement by re-reading an entire Issue thread. That is a lot of work and makes it so I need Dedicated Time® to review it, putting it forever in that "someday" category. That might sound like the ideal job for an agent. It will still take time to vet the sourcing and think through any analysis it has made. See also D-SUMMARIZE. A word on agentic development A large part of Rust's success is the effort in talking to people as humans. This has incidentally benefited Rust among agentic development as many of the needs overlap. I think continuing to focus on humans will be the best strategy in the long term, with the assumption that agents will continue to improve. Where examining the needs of agentic development can pay off is by seeing the same problems faced by humans but scaled to such a degree that it breaks us out of complacency with "good enough" 10% improvements. As I see it, the three pillars where humans and agents overlap are: Signal quality: One reason that Rust works well for agentic development is the feedback it provides. We need to clarify Cargo's existing signals by not being so overly verbose. We also need to provide more signals through tools like lints, audit points (think: unsafe), and so on. Dependency management: We also need to consider signals for selecting and auditing of dependencies as well as reducing the costs of having dependencies. Build performance: While a lot of agentic development is done in the background, the performance of the commands that agents run matters, especially if you want a tighter feedback loop (e.g. bun skipped cargo check in the first pass of its Rust port). The faster the operations are, the closer to the inner loop they will be used, and the better quality of results will be. Potential steps to this future While this list is long, it is not intended to be exhaustive. I got tired of writing. I am also less qualified to speak on some of these subjects or I don't have enough experience with them to speak too much about them. I frequently see the sentiment that nothing is being merged into Rust these days that justifies raising an MSRV. Looking over this list, I see a lot to get excited about. #[non_exhaustive] Maintainability async-ify Cargo Migrating away from libgit2 Resolving with PubGrub Generated shell completions Plumbing commands Structured logging Open namespaces Registry namespaces Public dependencies Battery packs Package distributions Mod templates Auditing Crate provenance Builtin dependencies lang:unsafe Declarative derive macros Proc-macro and build script access controls Reducing the need for build scripts Reducing user build scripts Proc-macro and build script allow list Cargo lints Test coverage API evolution Feature lifecycle API lifecycle Source inlining Auditing API changes Performance Improved decomposition Removing unnecessary rebuilds Shared caches Build cache GC Fine-grained cache locking Alternative compilation models Opaque dependencies Test result caching Iterating on test failures async-ify Cargo Cargo predates async / await and has its own bespoke async framework, using curl as the executor. This means Cargo can't leverage existing tooling around async executors, the code base does not follow familiar patterns for contributors, and takes a lot of work to then extend the code base to support running more things in parallel, like parsing of thousands of manifests. We'd also want to switch from curl to a Rust native networking library but this is one of a couple of pieces holding us back. Areas: Cargo maintenance Build performance Tracking issue: #16845 Migrating away from libgit2 When Cargo started, git was not deployed universally yet the Cargo team chose to use it as the transport mechanism for the registry index. libgit2 helped to fill this gap and made it possible to have a custom UX for progress. An escape hatch to use git was provided for any feature gaps users ran into. Over 10 years later, git is everywhere and no longer used for most Cargo registries. There is a high likelihood that those who have git dependencies will have git installed. It seems the right time to make the git escape hatch the default, improving fetch performance and network compatibility. Maybe we eventually remove the libgit2 network transport entirely. This would remove another dependency on curl, unblocking Cargo to switch to a Rust native networking library and a regular async executor. Maybe we can even remove libgit2 one day, either replacing it with gix or git, removing yet another C component from the build of Cargo. This will also reduce Cargo startup overhead. Areas Cargo maintenance Build performance Tracking issue: #17227 Resolving with PubGrub Cargo's dependency resolver has bugs, poor errors, and missing features. However, people don't feel confident making or reviewing changes It can also be difficult to know how to update the reference SAT implementation in the differential test suite. PubGrub is a generalized dependency resolver. We would be able to decouple the Cargo logic from the algorithm, making it easier to change and removing our need to do differential testing. The output is much richer, allowing for better errors. PubGrub has been proven out by Astral with uv, including the ease of making changes like changing how prerelease works. Areas Cargo maintenance Dependency management Tracking issue: #5284 Generated shell completions Cargo offers bash and zsh completions but these are written by hand with the expectation that any CLI changes are mirrored in these without a good testing story. Contributors and reviewers should not be expected to be bash and zsh completion experts or have every shell installed on their system. Cargo uses clap which offers generated completions but Cargo has some dynamically generated completions which clap only supports through an in-development feature. Stabilizing that feature and switching Cargo's completions over to the new system will make them more maintainable and more feature rich as it is much easier to provide dynamic completions with the new system. Areas: Cargo maintenance Tracking issue: #14520 Plumbing commands We want to break up cargo check into the smallest units of work possible and expose that as an API through a pipeline of plumbing commands. This would put callers in charge of what Cargo is doing, whether changing the data between steps to outright replacing steps with a custom implementation. By having this pipeline of operations with clear inputs/outputs between them, we'll by necessity need to do the same thing for the Cargo code base. For example, feature resolution would be an isolated, pure transformation from inputs to outputs. This makes it so contributors and reviewers have a finite area of concern to work with, making it easier to contribute and making reviewers more confident in accepting changes. Maybe one day, this refactoring will lead to breaking up Cargo into smaller libraries that people can use. There are trade offs with this though as it constrains the design within cargo, possibly makes it more complicated to abstract out CLI-specific assumptions, and locks callers into one version of cargo. I've maintained third-party tools that had called into cargo and it was annoying to users to get "unknown key" warnings or "this feature is unstable" errors (despite being stable within their toolchain). Plumbing commands should likely remain the assumed route for general purpose extensions. Areas: Cargo maintenance Adaptability Project Goal: Prototype a new set of Cargo “plumbing” commands Structured logging cargo check --timings can only show you how long that build took. Similarly, cargo check -v can only tell you why something rebuilt in that build. Many times, you don't know a build will be a problem until it is happening. With structured logging, you can get reports on previous builds to better diagnose problems. There is a large overlap in our needs for structured logging and programmatic output for our porcelain commands. In iterating on structured logging, we are also exploring how we can improve our programmatic output. Areas: Build performance Adaptability Tracking issue: #15844 Open namespaces In other languages, namespaces are explicit and open to extension. In Rust, they are coupled to the module system and closed to extension. This feature is about making Rust's namespaces partially open to extension where a another package can look as if it is a mod in another package. For example, take Clap: existing namepotential namenotes clapclap clap_deriveclap::derive clap_completeclap::complete clap_mangenclap::man clap_lexclap_lexfirst-party but a private dependency of clap clap-cargoclap-cargothird-party though an extension of clap's API This is more of a language feature impacting API design. This bleeds into dependency management in terms of providing an alternative to compose a cohesive API besides features, which have their drawbacks, and without coupling together the major version of all of the pieces, allowing for breaking changes with a smaller impact. This can further help dependency management if we extend the package UX in places like crates.io and docs.rs to make these navigable between them, extending the cohesion to our UX. Areas Dependency management Tracking issue: #13576 Registry namespaces There are many reasons people may want this. Within the scope of this document, the most relevant is knowing a package came from a trusted source and finding other packages from that source, like disjoint APIs from a company. Areas Dependency management Reference: Survey of organizational ownership and registry namespace designs for Cargo and Crates.io Public dependencies Being able to mark that a dependency (and its public dependencies) are part of your public API feels like a small, incremental improvement. At its most basic, it helps catch accidentally leaking dependencies in your public API. The most innocent example is an impl From<dep::Error> for Error. Tools, like cargo-semver-checks, can build on this to help identify unintended breaking changes by upgrading a dependency. It can be understandable to make a mistake and it helps to have tools catch the problem. Where this turns from a "you mistake" to a "systemic failure" is with workspace.dependencies. When changing them, it is easy to overlook where they are used. When preparing a library for release with an inherited dependency, you can no longer look at only the library to tell what all changed since the last release. I hesitate in further ingraining workspace.dependencies, like through cargo add (#10608), until this problem is solved as I fear we would be setting people up for failure. This also affects performance. If you want to generate documentation while developing, the simplest thing to do is cargo doc but that generates documentation for all dependencies, including slow to build dependencies like windows-sys. If you care to look, you may discover cargo doc --no-deps and maybe that will be good enough for you but happy paths shouldn't be gated by knowledge. With public dependencies, Cargo knows what dependencies are reachable by your project and can instead only generate documentation for those dependencies, speeding up your documentation builds. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issue: #44663 Package distributions Some packages need to be upgraded in lockstep and there isn't any tooling to assist with that today. We can improve this by allowing users to specify that a dependency's source comes from another dependency, like: [package] name = "some-cli" [dependencies] clap = { from = ["clap_complete", "clap_mangen"] } clap_complete = "4.6.0" clap_mangen = "4.6.0" That declaration is a bit backwards and could be improved with maintainers providing "distribution" packages: [package] name = "some-cli" [dependencies] clap_distribution = "4.6.0" clap.from = "clap_distribution" clap_complete.from = "clap_distribution" clap_mangen.from = "clap_distribution" This is starting to look similar to battery packs and could possibly be a way of upstreaming the concept into Cargo. Blocked on: Public dependencies Areas Dependency management Referenced at: RFC 3516: Future possibilities Mod templates cargo new only does whole-package generation from a fixed template. There are multiple kinds of templating though: Repo Package Crate Module Typically, these all get bundled together into repo or package templates (see also #5151), keeping the design scope quite large, making it harder to move a design forward for Cargo. One particular problem with repo templates is that they try to cover the needs of all of the other kinds of templates, either giving users a "full stack" application template that they then have to pare down to meet their needs or making the system complicated through templating logic and user prompts. We could extend cargo new with crate/module templates, leveraging examples as templates. Say you had a rust_cli package distribution with topical examples, you could startup a package with: $ cargo new --bin --from rust_cli:async_main $ cargo new --mod --from rust_cli:args $ cargo new --mod --from rust_cli:watch $ cargo new --test --from rust_cli:cli_tests $ fd Cargo.toml src/main.rs src/args.rs src/watch.rs tests/cli_tests.rs Note: this is only a rough sketch to highlight the idea What you get: Package metadata is inherited from a workspace, if it exists (already present) Dependencies populated from the given examples A runnable src/main.rs from the main example Additional modules that need to be edited and moded into src/main.rs You would still need to edit the various mods and mod them into src/main.rs Areas Dependency management Crate provenance The xz backdoor highlighted, among other problems, the danger of releases diverging from VCS. We need an audit point for when a published .crate file has no associated git sha, when it diverges from the source for that sha, and when that sha is an imposter commit. Areas Dependency management Referenced at: blog: 999 crates of Rust on the wall Builtin dependencies Identifying impure packages (those that can access files, the environment, networks, RNGs, etc) can serve as another audit point. We can get this through the build-std projects efforts to integrate dependencies on core, alloc, and std into Cargo's [dependencies]. This becomes especially important for proc-macros which your environment may run while you are reviewing a package and so Cargo can know if a run of a proc-macro is safe to cache, particularly if a caching system needs binary reproducibility which can be defeated by a simple HashMap. Of course, an alloc-only package only tells us some of the story due to unsafe, FFI, and asm!. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issue: #16960 lang:unsafe As just covered, even with alloc-only dependencies, there are still holes in our audit point coverage, like unsafe, FFI, and asm!. The idea here is to integrate access to language features into Cargo. One way we could do this is to migrate to where [features] could activate "lang:unsafe", e.g. [features] unsafe = ["lang:unsafe"] This wouldn't be to shame those packages but to serve as a higher level unsafe audit point accessible from the package's metadata and encourage providing safe-only alternative implementations for those who might not need some of the benefits gained by unsafe implementations. Of course, not every package can make use of unsafe optional and we would need to provide a way to work use unsafe with default-features = false. Maybe this could even be extended to language preview features (e.g. the proposed RFC 3965). While there is a lot of risk with allowing access to language features before stabilization, it would help if the default was for them to be opt-in by callers and easily discovered by the Rust Project. Areas Dependency management Build performance Declarative derive macros Even better would be declarative derive and attribute macros as the compiler will ensure they are pure. While these may not be able to handle every pure proc-macro case, every bit would help especially among foundational macros. This has the added bonus that there won't be a proc-macro crate and its dependencies that need building and linking, even in cargo check. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issue: rust#143549 Proc-macro and build script access controls Not all proc-macros can be pure. Build scripts can never be pure. But any problem with that is not specialized to these cases. You will eventually run the rest of a dependency's code with cargo test, cargo run, and with production deployment. What is special about proc-macros and build scripts is they are required to run to build the code. You might want to build as part of your auditing. Their non-determinism may impact caching solutions. We need to be able to have audit points for these impure operations. Even better if it can be extended towards tests. Even better if it also helps with regular dependencies. One approach is an access control system like Cackle. This would work for your entire build. Maybe Cargo can use OS features to restrict build script and proc-macros access as a way to highlight these audit points. Cargo should support a wide variety of OSs and they have different capabilities which may change with time, likely making enforcement be best-effort. We will need to provide some way for build scripts and proc-macros to specify the resources they wish to access. Maybe we could make this also work for tests and cargo run but it wouldn't help with deploying your production binary. Maybe we go all the way to a wasm sandbox. This is trivial for pure proc-macros though other ideas mentioned here will help. The big challenge is supporting what is needed by impure proc-macros as well as build scripts. Like with using OS enforcement, we will need a way to specify what resources can be accessed. Wasm sandboxing can likely lead to slower builds and not just because of having to run a wasm interpreter. Cargo goes out of its way to try to allow proc-macros and build scripts to reuse intermediate build artifacts with a user's application. When we've previously benchmarked diverging these builds more for "build performance", the results ended up being a wash because of the extra builds that happen. This is also limited in what it helps; it would not extend to your tests, cargo run, or your production binary. Areas Dependency management References: Cackle compiler-team#1017 Reducing the need for build scripts Cargo has provided build scripts as an escape hatch to allow rapid iteration without requiring upfront design work for first-class features within Cargo. Cargo would likely have failed without this. With hindsight, we can look back and identify patterns so we can design features to replace them, greatly reducing the use of build scripts. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issues: #14948 Reducing user build scripts Even when build scripts are still needed, it would help if we only had to audit one build script, rather than 20 build scripts that end up being wrappers around a library. This is the idea behind build script delegation. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issues: #14903 Proc-macro and build script allow list With enough of the above features, it wouldn't be too painful to make proc-macros and build scripts opt-in. For when a build script isn't opted into, maintainers could provide a fallback of a static set of build script directives to fill in just enough to move along on the happy path. I see two benefits here: Avoid accidentally running these before they are audited Faster builds for those who don't care about the benefits afforded by a build script Areas Dependency management Build performance Reference: Build script allowlist Cargo lints While clippy has a few lints for Cargo, it is at a disadvantage in terms of what data it has access to. Adding a linting system to Cargo would increase the number of quality signals users and agents can receive. These signals will improve the quality and build performance of dependencies. In particular, the linting system will come with built-in unused dependency detection. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issue: #12235 Test coverage To help improve the quality of your dependencies, we should have a paved path for test coverage reporting. I am also curious what the impact to agentic development would be to have first-class coverage reporting. I've observed that agent output can look good on the surface but it is in the small details where it is likely to fail. I have a theory that tests would amplify absurd output, making it easier to spot in review. I am unsure where all this might lead as there are problems with overly focusing on coverage. Areas Dependency management Tracking issue: #13040 Feature lifecycle Features exist or they don't. The act of adding a feature for what already exists is a breaking change. Maintainers need to be able to evolve the feature set of their library over time, minimizing breaking changes and helping users through breaking changes. We could even restrict language preview features (see lang:unsafe) to only unstable features, ensuring they remain opt-in. Areas Dependency management Tracking issues: #7130: Deprecating features #10881: Stable and unstable features API lifecycle Today, the only stable API lifecycle attribute is #[deprecated]. #[stable] and #[unstable] remain unstable, limiting them to only the standard library. Like with the idea of language preview features (see Feature lifecycle), we could make unstable APIs enabled through unstable features in Cargo, ensuring they remain opt-in. Areas Dependency management Reference: all-hands-2026#14 Source inlining While a #[deprecated(note)] helps with migrating off of an API, it is still a manual process. Migrating away from deprecated APIs is a manual process. The ideal would be like Editions where you run cargo fix and you are ready to go. While we may want to eventually allow maintainers to specify larger source transformations with #[deprecated], like what Coccinelle or ast-grep allow, Go's source inlining is likely to get us pretty far while being intuitive, easy to validate, and a small surface area to stabilize. Areas Dependency management Reference: blog: //go:fix inline and the source-level inliner Auditing API changes When reviewing a PR or making a release, it can be easy to overlook a breaking change. Conversely, we could do a better job exposing API changes to callers on upgrade to help them through migrations or to discover new features. There are multiple routes for improving this that need further exploration. Areas Dependency management Reference: cargo-public-api cargo-semver-checks/ Improved decomposition In C++, a .cpp file is the unit of compilation. Rust crates are a unit of compilation but the larger the compilation unit, the longer code-gen takes. This makes it so splitting crates can speed up compilation time at the cost of less visibility for optimizations though there is LTO to help with that. Splitting isn't without its costs: May run into limitations with the Orphan rules Loss of dead code detection More boilerplate to manage We either need to find an alternative way to express compilation units (e.g. "inline crates") or to remove the friction in managing an application split into crates. Some progress has been made on this, including workspace publishing workspace inheritance Areas Build performance Reference: hawk: A workspace-aware Cargo lint for unnecessary public Rust APIs. blog: Coherence and crate-level where-clauses Removing unnecessary rebuilds When you change a package in your dependency graph, you might not need to rebuild all dependents. In C++, the interface (stored in .h file) is kept separate from the implementation (in a .cpp file). There is more to this but it is enough of an explanation to serve our purposes. Each .cpp file gets its own intermediate build artifact. Each of these artifacts only needs to rebuild if a .h they depend on changes. We don't have this concept in Rust yet but maybe we can do better. The compiler already generates an .rmeta file for a package which is everything that is needed to build dependent, intermediate build artifacts without the need for the full .rlib. Cargo uses this today for what we call "pipelined compilation", where dependent builds can start in parallel to their dependency finalizing compilation. Could we get the same benefits of the .h / .cpp split, automatically? Yes, with a lot of a compiler work and some Cargo work. A polyfill already exists that demonstrates a portion of the build time improvements by replacing --workspace with the specific packages final artifacts that would be impacted. A real solution would be able to skip building some intermediate dependencies. This is a form of build output hashing. When applied more generally, Cargo can skip building artifacts, even linking, of dependents if the code change didn't change the output. However, this can only work for packages that are binary reproducible. Build scripts and proc-macros add some uncertainty here. Areas Build performance Tracking issue: #14604 Shared caches To share build caches across workspaces today, you need to share the build-dir. This is not without its downsides: This will serialize builds due to the locks. If something poisons the cache, you need to remove the entire cache to fix it This can interfere with incremental compilation Some cache entries will collide, causing extra rebuilds This is intentionally not documented by the Cargo team. If Cargo provided an append-only local cache for pure builds, a lot of these problems would be resolved. The main downside to a local cache is that you won't get much reuse. Just one dependency change can cause all dependents to have new cache entries. This isn't so much an issue for sharing a cache across multiple worktrees of the same repo. This would also be improved by having a remote cache that you trust, like the CI for the project you are contributing to. Why not pre-built binaries stored on crates.io? Besides issues of trust, almost no one would be able to use it. They have to be on the exact same version of every package in their dependency tree with the exact same features enabled with the exact same compiler flags with the exact same compiler version. More on this later. Areas Build performance Tracking issue: #5931 Build cache GC The more Cargo caches, the more disk space it eats up. Cargo needs to be a better citizen with respect to disk space. This becomes even more important in CI where any extra content cached with the CI provider is extra compression, upload, download, and decompression time wasted. Areas Build performance Tracking issue: #5026 Fine-grained cache locking Locking of the build-dir is all-or-nothing, causing contention between builds in a user's terminal and rust-analyzer or between git worktrees. Today, cache entries are mutable and read while still being written to (for pipelined compilation). Mutable entries give Cargo a cheap form of cache GC on local edits; without them Cargo would need a build cache GC to replace it. Solving that would help when switching between branches. Mutable entries also mean that Cargo does not need to know all build inputs a priori; we can look to other build systems that have already solved this problem. Areas Build performance Tracking issue: #4282 Alternative compilation models Zig will parse to AST, identify the entry points, like main, and then recurse until done. This is the ultimate form of dead code elimination where platform conditionals don't need to be viral. We use features for this today. They avoid needing to parse to AST but are difficult to work with and aren't as fine grained as Zig's builds. We have a polyfill present today in the form of -Zhint-mostly-unused. This only offers benefits in extreme cases (e.g. windows-sys) and still benefits from activating specific features. Another polyfill, cargo-slicer, has taken a couple different forms. One more extreme version would vendor your dependencies and strip them down to only what you used. Each time you change how you use a dependency, you must re-slice your dependencies which requires an initial build to identify what is used. This isn't an automatic win. The compiler would need to instead do the work of reducing unnecessary rebuilds. Cargo couldn't use local or remote caches. Compilation steps would become redundant between different binaries (like all tests). Areas Build performance Opaque dependencies Line for line and feature for feature, C++ and Rust may have similar compile times but you generally don't rebuild Unity from scratch while everyone does rebuild Bevy from scratch. You are also generally relinking all of Bevy as well. What Cargo is missing is a good story for working with dynamic libraries. Or in their more general form, opaque dependencies. Rust dependencies today are transparent like headers-only libraries in C++. Every detail of the dependency tree affects a developer's build. An opaque dependency appears to you as a single package, independent of how many packages it is made up of. An opaque dependency has an independent set of dependency versions and feature activations. No unification happens. On its own, this provides us a story for reducing link times. With a shared cache, this offers opportunities for more reuse across projects. Maybe we could even have pre-built opaque dependencies. With zig-style compilation, maybe compilation starts with main and the public functions of each opaque dependency, making this a hybrid between our current eager and zig's lazy builds, allowing for some artifacts to be cached. This also provides a way to avoid unifying features and dependencies, a long standing request. Areas Dependency management Build performance Tracking issue: #3573 Test result caching Cargo already has caching, including output, for builds. Cargo could do the same for tests so long as Cargo knew all of the inputs to a test binary. Areas Build performance Iterating on test failures If we are more directly integrating libtest with cargo test, Cargo can do basic things like running multiple test binaries at once. We can go a step further and define new workflows. For myself, I frequently run cargo test, figure out how to call the failure I'm focusing on, iterate until it passes, and then work on the next. If Cargo had a fail-fast / run-failures-first mode, this would remove a lot of friction to people having a faster test loop. Areas Build performance

sentences.en: They are iterating on test failures until they get the behavior just right, either running all of cargo test --workspace in a loop ("because it's easy") or hand constructing a command like cargo test -p application-library --test area -- some::test::name for each failure to give faster iteration time at the cost of a disruption.
sentences.zh: 他们对测试失败进行迭代，直到获得正确的行为，或者在循环中运行所有的cargo test --workspace（“因为它很容易”），或者手动构建一个像cargo test -p application-library --test area -- some::test::name 这样的命令，为每个失败提供更快的迭代时间，但以中断为代价。

blocks.html_en: Maybe while working through either of the above, they rebase against main and now their whole stack is rebuilding because of a dependency update. Or maybe they ran out of disk space and had to run rm -rf target. Or maybe it rebuilt for no discernible reason.

sentences.en: Maybe while working through either of the above, they rebase against main and now their whole stack is rebuilding because of a dependency update.

sentences.en: Or maybe they ran out of disk space and had to run rm -rf target.
sentences.zh: 或者，他们可能耗尽了磁盘空间，不得不运行 rm -rf target。

sentences.en: Or maybe it rebuilt for no discernible reason.
sentences.zh: 或者也许它的重建没有明显的原因。

blocks.html_en: Or maybe while working through either of the above, Cargo blocks on a parallel invocation, whether from rust-analyzer, another worktree they want to share the cache with, or from another project on their system that they are sharing the cache with.

sentences.en: Or maybe while working through either of the above, Cargo blocks on a parallel invocation, whether from rust-analyzer, another worktree they want to share the cache with, or from another project on their system that they are sharing the cache with.

blocks.html_en: Cargo is intended to be opinionated but between that and backwards compatibility, it can be hard to be adaptable to different needs, whether that is improved docker caching, complex application needs, or integrating into a larger corporate environment.

sentences.en: Cargo is intended to be opinionated but between that and backwards compatibility, it can be hard to be adaptable to different needs, whether that is improved docker caching, complex application needs, or integrating into a larger corporate environment.
sentences.zh: Cargo 的目的是固执己见，但在向后兼容性之间，它可能很难适应不同的需求，无论是改进的 Docker 缓存、复杂的应用程序需求，还是集成到更大的企业环境中。

blocks.html_en: In git, they divide operations into plumbing and porcelain. Cargo is almost all porcelain commands with very limited programmatic use. Adding plumbing commands and extending the programmatic output of the porcelain commands would go a long way to enabling people to adapt Cargo to meet their needs.

sentences.en: In git, they divide operations into plumbing and porcelain.
sentences.zh: 在 git 中，他们将操作分为管道和瓷器。

sentences.en: Cargo is almost all porcelain commands with very limited programmatic use.

sentences.en: Adding plumbing commands and extending the programmatic output of the porcelain commands would go a long way to enabling people to adapt Cargo to meet their needs.

blocks.html_en: Underlying any talk of improving Cargo is that the Cargo team needs enough capacity to support these efforts on top of keeping the lights on. sentences.en: I worry about how close we are to repeating that.

blocks.html_en: During that feature freeze and for a while after, we had a focus on improving our processes and tooling to make us more effective in maintaining Cargo. For example, we made it easier to make sweeping UX changes by developing and migrating to a snapshot testing library that met our needs (snapbox, see #14039).

sentences.en: During that feature freeze and for a while after, we had a focus on improving our processes and tooling to make us more effective in maintaining Cargo.
sentences.zh: 在功能冻结期间和之后的一段时间内，我们专注于改进我们的流程和工具，以使我们更有效地维护 Cargo。

sentences.en: For example, we made it easier to make sweeping UX changes by developing and migrating to a snapshot testing library that met our needs (snapbox, see #14039).
sentences.zh: 例如，我们通过开发并迁移到满足我们需求的快照测试库（snapbox，请参阅#14039），使彻底的用户体验更改变得更容易。

blocks.html_en: Now, the thing I see slowing us down the most and limiting what we change is Cargo's architecture. Cargo is old and has bespoke frameworks, constraints on concurrent operations, uses C libraries when Rust ones can replace them, and no clear boundaries that require global knowledge when making or reviewing a change.

sentences.en: Now, the thing I see slowing us down the most and limiting what we change is Cargo's architecture.
sentences.zh: 现在，我认为最拖慢我们速度并限制我们改变的就是 Cargo 的架构。

sentences.en: Cargo is old and has bespoke frameworks, constraints on concurrent operations, uses C libraries when Rust ones can replace them, and no clear boundaries that require global knowledge when making or reviewing a change.
sentences.zh: Cargo 很旧，有定制的框架，对并发操作的限制，在 Rust 库可以替代它们时使用 C 库，并且在进行或审查更改时没有需要全局知识的明确界限。

blocks.html_en: Not everyone can fund work like that and we can only build up new design and code reviewers so quickly. Where outside contributors can most help the Cargo team is not with code but with thinking. A major enabler for thinking is to have all the context in one place by gathering all of the relevant information from the thread and summarizing it for easy consumption. For example, I have a PR on another project that slowly makes progress and when I go back to look at it, I have to refresh myself on the behavior the PR is intended to implement by re-reading an entire Issue thread. That is a lot of work and makes it so I need Dedicated Time® to review it, putting it forever in that "someday" category. That might sound like the ideal job for an agent. It will still take time to vet the sourcing and think through any analysis it has made. See also D-SUMMARIZE.

sentences.en: A word on agentic development
sentences.zh: 关于代理开发的一句话

blocks.html_en: A large part of Rust's success is the effort in talking to people as humans. This has incidentally benefited Rust among agentic development as many of the needs overlap. I think continuing to focus on humans will be the best strategy in the long term, with the assumption that agents will continue to improve. Where examining the needs of agentic development can pay off is by seeing the same problems faced by humans but scaled to such a degree that it breaks us out of complacency with "good enough" 10% improvements.

sentences.en: A large part of Rust's success is the effort in talking to people as humans.
sentences.zh: Rust 的成功很大程度上归功于以人的方式与人交谈所付出的努力。

sentences.en: This has incidentally benefited Rust among agentic development as many of the needs overlap.
sentences.zh: 由于许多需求重叠，这无意中使 Rust 在代理开发中受益。

sentences.en: I think continuing to focus on humans will be the best strategy in the long term, with the assumption that agents will continue to improve.
sentences.zh: 我认为，从长远来看，继续关注人类将是最好的策略，前提是智能体将继续改进。

sentences.en: Where examining the needs of agentic development can pay off is by seeing the same problems faced by humans but scaled to such a degree that it breaks us out of complacency with "good enough" 10% improvements.
sentences.zh: 检查代理开发的需求可以得到回报，那就是看到人类面临的相同问题，但规模扩大到这样的程度，使我们不再自满于“足够好”的 10% 改进。

blocks.html_en: Signal quality: One reason that Rust works well for agentic development is the feedback it provides. We need to clarify Cargo's existing signals by not being so overly verbose. We also need to provide more signals through tools like lints, audit points (think: unsafe), and so on.

sentences.en: Signal quality: One reason that Rust works well for agentic development is the feedback it provides.
sentences.zh: 信号质量：Rust 适合代理开发的原因之一是它提供的反馈。

sentences.en: We need to clarify Cargo's existing signals by not being so overly verbose.
sentences.zh: 我们需要澄清 Cargo 的现有信号，不要过于冗长。

sentences.en: We also need to provide more signals through tools like lints, audit points (think: unsafe), and so on.
sentences.zh: 我们还需要通过 lint、审核点（认为：不安全）等工具提供更多信号。

blocks.html_en: Dependency management: We also need to consider signals for selecting and auditing of dependencies as well as reducing the costs of having dependencies.

sentences.en: Dependency management: We also need to consider signals for selecting and auditing of dependencies as well as reducing the costs of having dependencies.
sentences.zh: 依赖关系管理：我们还需要考虑用于选择和审核依赖关系的信号以及降低依赖关系的成本。

blocks.html_en: Build performance: While a lot of agentic development is done in the background, the performance of the commands that agents run matters, especially if you want a tighter feedback loop (e.g. bun skipped cargo check in the first pass of its Rust port). The faster the operations are, the closer to the inner loop they will be used, and the better quality of results will be.

sentences.en: Build performance: While a lot of agentic development is done in the background, the performance of the commands that agents run matters, especially if you want a tighter feedback loop (e.g. bun skipped cargo check in the first pass of its Rust port).
sentences.zh: 构建性能：虽然许多代理开发是在后台完成的，但代理运行的命令的性能很重要，特别是如果您想要更紧密的反馈循环（例如，在 Rust 端口的第一遍中，bun 跳过了货物检查）。

sentences.en: The faster the operations are, the closer to the inner loop they will be used, and the better quality of results will be.
sentences.zh: 运算速度越快，它们就越接近内循环，结果的质量就越好。

blocks.html_en: When Cargo started, git was not deployed universally yet the Cargo team chose to use it as the transport mechanism for the registry index. libgit2 helped to fill this gap and made it possible to have a custom UX for progress. An escape hatch to use git was provided for any feature gaps users ran into.

sentences.en: When Cargo started, git was not deployed universally yet the Cargo team chose to use it as the transport mechanism for the registry index.
sentences.zh: 当 Cargo 启动时，git 尚未普遍部署，但 Cargo 团队选择使用它作为注册表索引的传输机制。

sentences.en: libgit2 helped to fill this gap and made it possible to have a custom UX for progress.

sentences.en: An escape hatch to use git was provided for any feature gaps users ran into.

blocks.html_en: Over 10 years later, git is everywhere and no longer used for most Cargo registries. There is a high likelihood that those who have git dependencies will have git installed. It seems the right time to make the git escape hatch the default, improving fetch performance and network compatibility.

sentences.en: In C++, the interface (stored in .h file) is kept separate from the implementation (in a .cpp file).
sentences.zh: 在 C++ 中，接口（存储在 .h 文件中）与实现（在 .cpp 文件中）分开。

sentences.en: We don't have this concept in Rust yet but maybe we can do better.
sentences.zh: 我们在 Rust 中还没有这个概念，但也许我们可以做得更好。

sentences.en: The compiler already generates an .rmeta file for a package which is everything that is needed to build dependent, intermediate build artifacts without the need for the full .rlib.
sentences.zh: 编译器已经为包生成了一个 .rmeta 文件，该文件包含构建依赖的中间构建工件所需的一切，而无需完整的 .rlib。

sentences.en: Cargo uses this today for what we call "pipelined compilation", where dependent builds can start in parallel to their dependency finalizing compilation.

blocks.html_en: If Cargo provided an append-only local cache for pure builds, a lot of these problems would be resolved.

sentences.en: If Cargo provided an append-only local cache for pure builds, a lot of these problems would be resolved.
sentences.zh: 如果 Cargo 为纯构建提供仅附加的本地缓存，那么很多问题都将得到解决。

blocks.html_en: The main downside to a local cache is that you won't get much reuse. Just one dependency change can cause all dependents to have new cache entries. This isn't so much an issue for sharing a cache across multiple worktrees of the same repo.

sentences.en: The main downside to a local cache is that you won't get much reuse.
sentences.zh: 本地缓存的主要缺点是您不会得到太多的重用。

sentences.en: Just one dependency change can cause all dependents to have new cache entries.
sentences.zh: 只需一项依赖项更改即可导致所有依赖项拥有新的缓存条目。

sentences.en: This isn't so much an issue for sharing a cache across multiple worktrees of the same repo.
sentences.zh: 对于在同一存储库的多个工作树之间共享缓存来说，这并不是什么大问题。

content_html_zh:
根据 Stack Overflow 的说法，cargo 是最理想的开发工具。 许多人将 Rust 的选择归功于 Cargo。 我从很多人那里听说 Cargo 已经很棒了，但他们想不出任何可以改进的方法。 我想把我们的目光放得更高。

我想听听您对理想工作流程是什么样子以及我们如何实现这一目标的想法。 这只是我一直在思考的一些事情。 我知道我不知道或无法轻易谈论所有工作流程，其他人可能对如何解决它们有更好的想法。

我们还可以利用您的帮助来实现这一目标。 这些工作流程不仅限于 Cargo，还涉及 Rust、crates.io 等。 有很多机会可以挖掘和提供帮助。

一些需要改进的工作流程

我想围绕工作流程的高级视图来构建这次讨论。 我将介绍特定的问题领域（例如构建脚本），作为如何改进它们的想法的一部分。

#[非详尽]

另外，关于代理开发的一句话

依赖管理

“永远把赌注押在生态系统上”

- 电池组：我们来谈谈板条箱吧，宝贝

我强烈地感觉到 crates.io 生态系统一直是 Rust 的超级力量之一，它使应用程序能够快速创建，并且比没有这个生态系统时具有更多的功能和完善。

应用程序不仅可以利用现有功能，还可以利用任何未来的功能和修复。 例如，ripgrep 正在针对大型 monorepos 进行优化，并且由于重用忽略而自动出现打字错误。 新的实现或分叉不会带来这样的好处。 这还可以实现共享审核。 在您的应用程序中，您可以拥有一两个也可供其他人使用的序列化框架，或者您可以审核分布在配置系统、网络通信等方面的十个定制框架。

依赖性并非没有成本和风险，我们应该努力降低这些成本和风险。

您如何发现质量依赖性？

假设您了解情况，可以使用“已知”依赖项。 生产力不应该受到内部知识的限制。

当不存在“已知”依赖性时，您就需要寻找候选者，而这并不总是那么容易。 为了比较它们，您可以寻找一些信号来看看它是否安全、适合您的目的以及可以长期依赖。 这些可能包括下载计数、依赖它的人、执行的评论等，以及从作者的其他软件包继承的信任。 了解并汇总这些可能需要大量工作。

在理想的世界中，所有依赖关系都将被审查。 我们并不处于一个理想的世界，但我们如何才能接近理想的世界呢？ 在 Rust 中，我们使用 unsafe 作为隔离需要进一步检查的代码的方法。 我们需要更多类型的审计点并扩大其可发现性。 如果您不需要审查这些审核点就更好了，因为它们是在可能的情况下选择加入的，并且不需要以性能或功能为代价进行审核。 但有时，我们仍然希望走捷径并信任其他人进行评论，并且对我们自己或其他人的评论的跟踪应与使用依赖项相结合。

我们如何最大限度地减少升级开销？

首先，我们需要改进维护人员的检查和测试状态，以减少错误和意外更改。

假设我们现在正在讨论预期的更改，简单的答案是阻止破坏性更改，但这会给维护人员带来代价，因为他们无法清除某些类型的技术债务，而用户也会受到功能、修复和构建性能的限制。

我们应该鼓励记录变化并更好地表现出来。 然而，这是解决问题的权宜之计。 我们怎样才能让这件事变得更好？

灵感的一个来源是 Rust 语言，它也有一种通过版本选择加入突破性更改的形式。 Rust 项目准备推出具有不稳定功能的版本，并为用户提供迁移。 这应该被视为我们为软件包的维护者和用户提供的最低体验。 除此之外，我们可以更好地向用户展示这些更改，使其符合他们的工作流程并针对他们的具体情况。 当无法进行迁移时，这一点尤其重要。

作为今天可以做什么的实验，通过 clap，我采用了将破坏性更改作为并行功能引入的做法，弃用了旧行为，并在可能的情况下注释了如何迁移。 这些弃用功能已被置于弃用功能标志后面，因为许多人将警告转化为错误（包括弃用功能），并且默认启用它们，同时升级并解决弃用功能会增加成本和风险。 这极大地简化了“启用功能并按照其说明进行操作”的迁移指南。 在无法实现并行功能的情况下，我们使用不稳定的 vX 功能来不阻止最终重大更改的开发，并更容易获得反馈。

我看到的问题是：

  • 了解已弃用的功能
  • 发现迁移指南
  • 迁移仍然是手动的
  • 不稳定的vX功能可能会产生令人惊讶的效果，并且需要更多的护栏来扩大其使用范围
  • 这些只是我编造的惯例；维持围绕这些想法的文化需要铺平道路来提高认识并鼓励其使用

构建性能

提高构建性能并不是让速度提高 2%，而是改变用户的工作方式并使 Rust 对更多用户有吸引力。 用户的比较点范围从 C++（在考虑预构建框架之前更相似）到脚本语言（没有构建）。

我们还需要超越 rustc 的性能，关注用户的工作流程。

用户在堆栈底部进行微小更改时寻求即时反馈，但不幸的是，这会导致整个堆栈重建，甚至需要一些时间进行货物检查。

他们对测试失败进行迭代，直到获得正确的行为，或者在循环中运行所有的cargo test --workspace（“因为它很容易”），或者手动构建一个像cargo test -p application-library --test area -- some::test::name 这样的命令，为每个失败提供更快的迭代时间，但以中断为代价。

也许在完成上述任一操作时，他们会针对 main 进行变基，现在由于依赖项更新，他们的整个堆栈正在重建。 或者，他们可能耗尽了磁盘空间，不得不运行 rm -rf target。 或者也许它的重建没有明显的原因。

或者，在执行上述任一操作时，Cargo 会阻塞并行调用，无论是来自 rust-analyzer（他们想要与之共享缓存的另一个工作树），还是来自他们系统上与其共享缓存的另一个项目。

一些用户会在等待 CI 完成时进行任务切换，这样他们就不会在未合并的代码之上堆叠太多更改，从而增加代价高昂的合并冲突的风险。 CI 系统有缓存，但缓存太多可能会抵消网络传输和解压缩时间带来的任何好处。 适合本地调试的默认设置会增加缓存大小并减慢构建速度。 虽然构建结果会被缓存，但测试结果不会被缓存，并且整个测试套件会重新运行。

适应性

Cargo 的目的是固执己见，但在向后兼容性之间，它可能很难适应不同的需求，无论是改进的 Docker 缓存、复杂的应用程序需求，还是集成到更大的企业环境中。

在 git 中，他们将操作分为管道和瓷器。 Cargo 几乎都是瓷器命令，编程用途非常有限。 添加管道命令和扩展瓷器命令的编程输出将大大有助于人们适应 Cargo 以满足他们的需求。

货物维护

任何有关改进 Cargo 的讨论的根本原因是，除了保持正常运转之外，Cargo 团队还需要足够的能力来支持这些工作。 此前，由于团队能力不足，Cargo 经历了几年的功能冻结。 我担心我们离重蹈覆辙还有多远。

在功能冻结期间和之后的一段时间内，我们专注于改进我们的流程和工具，以使我们更有效地维护 Cargo。 例如，我们通过开发并迁移到满足我们需求的快照测试库（snapbox，请参阅#14039），使彻底的用户体验更改变得更容易。

现在，我认为最拖慢我们速度并限制我们改变的就是 Cargo 的架构。 Cargo 很旧，有定制的框架，对并发操作的限制，在 Rust 库可以替代它们时使用 C 库，并且在进行或审查更改时没有需要全局知识的明确界限。

不是每个人都能资助这样的工作，我们只能如此迅速地建立新的设计和代码审查人员。 外部贡献者对 Cargo 团队最有帮助的不是代码，而是思考。 思考的一个主要推动因素是通过从线程中收集所有相关信息并对其进行总结以方便使用，从而将所有上下文集中在一个地方。 例如，我在另一个项目上有一个 PR，该项目进展缓慢，当我回去查看它时，我必须通过重新阅读整个问题线程来刷新自己以了解 PR 旨在实现的行为。 这是一项繁重的工作，因此我需要 Dedicated Time® 来审查它，将其永远放在“有一天”类别中。 这听起来可能是经纪人的理想工作。 审查来源并思考其所做的任何分析仍然需要时间。 另请参见 D-SUMMARIZE。

关于代理开发的一句话

Rust 的成功很大程度上归功于以人的方式与人交谈所付出的努力。 由于许多需求重叠，这无意中使 Rust 在代理开发中受益。 我认为，从长远来看，继续关注人类将是最好的策略，前提是智能体将继续改进。 检查代理开发的需求可以得到回报，那就是看到人类面临的相同问题，但规模扩大到这样的程度，使我们不再自满于“足够好”的 10% 改进。

在我看来，人类和智能体重叠的三大支柱是：

信号质量：Rust 适合代理开发的原因之一是它提供的反馈。 我们需要澄清 Cargo 的现有信号，不要过于冗长。 我们还需要通过 lint、审核点（认为：不安全）等工具提供更多信号。

依赖关系管理：我们还需要考虑用于选择和审核依赖关系的信号以及降低依赖关系的成本。

构建性能：虽然许多代理开发是在后台完成的，但代理运行的命令的性能很重要，特别是如果您想要更紧密的反馈循环（例如，在 Rust 端口的第一遍中，bun 跳过了货物检查）。 运算速度越快，它们就越接近内循环，结果的质量就越好。

异步货物

Cargo 早于 async/await 并拥有自己定制的异步框架，使用curl作为执行器。

这意味着 Cargo 无法利用围绕异步执行器的现有工具，代码库不遵循贡献者熟悉的模式，并且需要大量工作来扩展代码库以支持并行运行更多内容，例如解析数千个清单。

我们还想从curl切换到Rust本机网络库，但这只是阻碍我们的几个因素之一。

跟踪问题：#16845

从 libgit2 迁移

当 Cargo 启动时，git 尚未普遍部署，但 Cargo 团队选择使用它作为注册表索引的传输机制。 libgit2 帮助填补了这一空白，并使自定义用户体验取得进展成为可能。 为用户遇到的任何功能缺陷提供了使用 git 的逃生口。

十多年后，git 无处不在，并且大多数 Cargo 注册中心不再使用它。 那些有 git 依赖的人很可能会安装 git。 现在似乎是时候将 git escape hide 设置为默认值，从而提高获取性能和网络兼容性。

也许我们最终会完全删除 libgit2 网络传输。 这将消除对curl的另一个依赖，解锁Cargo以切换到Rust本机网络库和常规异步执行器。

也许有一天我们甚至可以删除 libgit2，用 gix 或 git 替换它，从 Cargo 的构建中删除另一个 C 组件。 这也将减少 Cargo 的启动开销。

跟踪问题：#17227

使用 PubGrub 解决

Cargo 的依赖解析器存在错误、严重错误和缺失功能。 然而，人们对做出或审查更改没有信心。也可能很难知道如何更新差异测试套件中的参考 SAT 实现。

PubGrub 是一个通用的依赖解析器。 我们将能够将 Cargo 逻辑与算法分离，使其更容易更改并消除我们进行差异测试的需要。 输出更加丰富，允许更好的错误。

PubGrub 已通过 Astral 与 uv 的验证，包括易于进行更改，例如更改预发布的工作方式。

生成的 shell 补全

Cargo 提供 bash 和 zsh 补全，但这些都是手工编写的，期望任何 CLI 更改都会在没有良好测试故事的情况下反映在其中。 贡献者和审阅者不应成为 bash 和 zsh 补全专家，也不应期望其系统上安装了所有 shell。

Cargo 使用 clap 提供生成的补全，但 Cargo 有一些动态生成的补全，而 clap 仅通过正在开发的功能支持。 稳定该功能并将 Cargo 的补全切换到新系统将使它们更易于维护且功能更丰富，因为使用新系统提供动态补全要容易得多。

我们希望将货物检查分解为尽可能小的工作单元，并通过管道命令管道将其公开为 API。 这将使调用者负责 Cargo 正在执行的操作，无论是更改步骤之间的数据还是用自定义实现彻底替换步骤。

语言：不安全

正如刚才所介绍的，即使使用仅分配依赖项，我们的审计点覆盖率仍然存在漏洞，例如 unsafe、FFI 和 asm!。 这里的想法是将语言功能的访问集成到 Cargo 中。

我们可以做到这一点的一种方法是迁移到 [features] 可以激活“lang:unsafe”的位置，例如

[features]
unsafe = ["lang:unsafe"]

这并不是要羞辱这些包，而是作为可从包的元数据访问的更高级别的不安全审计点，并鼓励为那些可能不需要不安全实现所带来的一些好处的人提供仅安全的替代实现。 当然，并不是每个包都可以使用 unsafe 可选，我们需要提供一种在 default-features = false 的情况下使用 unsafe 的方法。

也许这甚至可以扩展到语言预览功能（例如提议的 RFC 3965）。 虽然在稳定之前允许访问语言功能存在很大的风险，但如果默认情况下它们由调用者选择加入并且很容易被 Rust 项目发现，那将会有所帮助。

当您更改依赖关系图中的包时，您可能不需要重建所有依赖项。

在 C++ 中，接口（存储在 .h 文件中）与实现（在 .cpp 文件中）分开。 虽然还有更多内容，但这足以解释我们的目的。 每个 .cpp 文件都有自己的中间构建工件。 这些工件中的每一个仅当它们依赖于更改时才需要重建。

我们在 Rust 中还没有这个概念，但也许我们可以做得更好。 编译器已经为包生成了一个 .rmeta 文件，该文件包含构建依赖的中间构建工件所需的一切，而无需完整的 .rlib。 Cargo 今天将其用于我们所说的“管道编译”，其中依赖构建可以与其依赖项最终编译并行启动。

这是构建输出散列的一种形式。 当更广泛地应用时，如果代码更改没有改变输出，Cargo 可以跳过依赖项的构建工件，甚至链接。 但是，这仅适用于二进制可重现的包。 构建脚本和过程宏在这里增加了一些不确定性。

本地缓存的主要缺点是您不会得到太多的重用。 只需一项依赖项更改即可导致所有依赖项拥有新的缓存条目。 对于在同一存储库的多个工作树之间共享缓存来说，这并不是什么大问题。

通过拥有您信任的远程缓存（例如您所贡献的项目的 CI）也可以改善这一点。

为什么不将预构建的二进制文件存储在 crates.io 上？ 除了信任问题之外，几乎没有人能够使用它。 它们必须位于其依赖树中每个包的完全相同的版本上，并且使用完全相同的编译器标志和完全相同的编译器版本启用完全相同的功能。 稍后会详细介绍这一点。

替代编译模型

Zig 将解析为 AST，识别入口点（如 main），然后递归直至完成。 这是消除死代码的最终形式，其中平台条件不需要病毒式传播。

今天我们使用此功能。 它们避免了解析 AST 的需要，但很难使用，并且不像 Zig 的构建那样细粒度。

今天我们有一个以 -Zhint- 大部分未使用的形式出现的 Polyfill。 这仅在极端情况下（例如 windows-sys）提供好处，并且仍然可以从激活特定功能中受益。

另一种填充物，货物切片机，有几种不同的形式。 一种更极端的版本会提供您的依赖项，并将它们精简为仅您使用的内容。 每次更改依赖项的使用方式时，都必须重新切片依赖项，这需要初始构建来识别所使用的内容。

这不是自动获胜。 编译器需要减少不必要的重建。 Cargo 无法使用本地或远程缓存。 不同二进制文件之间的编译步骤将变得多余（就像所有测试一样）。

不透明的依赖关系

一行接一行，功能接功能，C++ 和 Rust 可能具有相似的编译时间，但您通常不会从头开始重建 Unity，而每个人都会从头开始重建 Bevy。 您通常也会重新链接所有 Bevy。 Cargo 缺少的是一个使用动态库的好故事。 或者以更一般的形式，不透明的依赖关系。

如今，Rust 依赖关系是透明的，就像 C++ 中的仅头文件库一样。 依赖树的每个细节都会影响开发人员的构建。

不透明的依赖项在您看来是一个单独的包，与它由多少个包组成无关。 不透明依赖项具有一组独立的依赖项版本和功能激活。 没有统一发生。

就其本身而言，这为我们提供了一个减少链接时间的故事。 通过共享缓存，这提供了跨项目更多重用的机会。 也许我们甚至可以预先构建不透明的依赖关系。 使用 Zig 风格的编译，也许编译从每个不透明依赖项的 main 和公共函数开始，使其成为我们当前的 eager 和 Zig 的惰性构建之间的混合体，从而允许缓存一些工件。

这也提供了一种避免统一功能和依赖项的方法，这是一个长期存在的要求。
